To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the posterior contraction rate in Gaussian process regression is the same as the contraction rate of the leading coefficients in a Karhunne--Lo\'{o}ve expansion of a Gaussian process.
posterior contraction rates can be derived for Gaussian process regression using a Gaussian approximation in the $W_2$-Wasserstein distance.
we develop an approximation to the posterior distribution using the Wasserstein distance, and use this approximation to obtain posterior contraction rates in Gaussian process regression.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our results provide an alternative approach to the posterior contraction rates in Gaussian process regression, and the approach may be applicable to other problems in Bayesian nonparametrics.

, for Gaussian processes with unbounded domain, posterior rates of contraction can be derived in terms of the Wasserstein distance, which is a distance between measures, and the Wasserstein distance can be related to the $L^1$ distance, which is an $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ distance between functions, by means of an appropriate coupling argument.
our work provides a posterior contraction result for a wide range of Gaussian processes with unbounded covariates, including the Gaussian and squared-exponential covariance kernels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the posterior contraction rate is $n^{-2/3}$, where $n$ denotes the number of observations, for the squared-exponential kernel and the rate is $n^{1/2}$ for the Gaussian kernel.
we establish posterior contraction for Gaussian process regression with the squared-exponential kernel under the Wasserstein metric.
, in the Gaussian process regression setting, we establish the first non-asymptotic posterior contraction result with a rate that is not a function of the dimension of the covariate domain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the $L^1$ Wasserstein approximation of a posterior distribution can be used to study the posterior contraction in unbounded domains.

, for Gaussian process regression with a squared-exponential kernel, a rate of $O(n^{-1/3})$ can be achieved, where $n$ is the sample size, which is faster than the rate $O(n^{-2/5})$ that can be obtained using the standard Gaussian approximation in the $d$-dimensional Hellinger metric.
the $L^p$ Wasserstein distance, for $p\geq 1$, is an appropriate tool for analyzing contraction in Gaussian process posterior distributions.
